sedetani.t: An Iberian people of the middle Ebro around Salduie, the native town on whose site Augustus founded Caesaraugusta, modern Zaragoza.
sedetani.o: The Sedetani occupied the middle Ebro valley around modern Zaragoza from at least the 5th century BCE. They belonged to the Iberian world, with fortified towns on hills and terraces above the river and its tributaries.
sedetani.r: Their main centre was Salduie, which minted coins with the Iberian legend Salduie. Farming of the fertile Ebro plain, livestock and trade along the river underpinned their economy. They are sometimes confused in ancient texts with the Edetani of Valencia. Horsemen from Salduie served Rome in the Social War and received citizenship in 89 BCE, recorded on the Bronze of Ascoli.
sedetani.e: The Sedetani were brought under Roman control during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and became part of Hispania Citerior. Around 14 BCE Augustus founded the colony of Caesaraugusta on the site of Salduie, and the Sedetani merged into Roman provincial society.

selinous.t: The westernmost Greek city in Sicily, famed for its great temples, which was destroyed by Carthage in 409 BCE.
selinous.o: Colonists from Megara Hyblaea, led by Pammilus, founded Selinous around 628 BCE on a coastal plateau between two rivers in south-western Sicily, according to Thucydides; some ancient sources give an earlier date. The name came from wild celery (selinon), which appears on its coins.
selinous.r: Selinous grew rich from its grain-growing lands and trade with Carthage and the Elymians, and it built more large temples than almost any other Greek city: on its acropolis and on the eastern hill stand the remains of at least eight, including the colossal Temple G, and their sculpted metopes are now in Palermo. It sided with Carthage in 480 BCE but later quarrelled over borders with Segesta, which called in Athens and Carthage.
selinous.e: In 409 BCE a Carthaginian army under Hannibal Mago stormed Selinous after nine days, killing thousands. The city revived under Carthaginian control, but in 250 BCE Carthage moved its inhabitants to Lilybaeum and abandoned it. Its archaeological park is one of the largest in Europe.

sequani.t: Gallic people of Franche-Comté whose rivalry with the Aedui led them to invite the German Ariovistus into Gaul.
sequani.o: The Sequani lived between the Saône, the Jura and the Rhine, around their great oppidum of Vesontio (Besançon) in a loop of the Doubs. Their land was famous for salted pork exported to Rome.
sequani.r: They contested with the Aedui for control of tolls on the Saône and for leadership of Gaul. Caesar names Catamantaloedes as a former king who held the title of friend of the Roman people, and his son Casticus as a would-be king.
sequani.e: To defeat the Aedui they hired the German leader Ariovistus, who then seized a third of their land, until Caesar drove him out in 58 BCE. The Sequani joined the revolt of 52 BCE. Under Rome Vesontio became an important town, and their land later formed the province of Maxima Sequanorum.

second-taifa-of-cordoba.t: Córdoba's brief independence under the qadi Ibn Hamdin during the collapse of Almoravid rule in al-Andalus in the 1140s.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.o: In 1144, amid revolts across al-Andalus against the Almoravids, the Córdoban qadi Ibn Hamdin, from a leading family of jurists, was proclaimed emir by the city's notables and expelled the Almoravid garrison.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.r: Ibn Hamdin's authority rested on his religious office and local support rather than on an army. He briefly claimed recognition from other cities, but was driven out for a time by the Hudid prince Zafadola and had to seek help from Alfonso VII of Castile, while the Almoravid commander Yahya ibn Ghaniya fought to retake the city.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.e: Ibn Hamdin fled to North Africa, and by 1148 Córdoba had passed to the Almohads, who made Seville their main Andalusi capital. Córdoba fell to Ferdinand III of the Crown of Castile in 1236.

senones.t: Gallic people of the Yonne around Sens, a branch of whom sacked Rome in about 390 BCE and settled on the Adriatic coast.
senones.o: The Senones held the land along the Yonne and the upper Seine, with Agedincum (Sens) as their chief town. Livy and Polybius record that part of the people crossed the Alps around 400 BCE; led by Brennus, they defeated the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome, then settled on the Adriatic coast around Sena Gallica (Senigallia).
senones.r: In Gaul they were a powerful people with a council of nobles. Caesar made Cavarinus their king, but the Senones drove him out in 54 BCE, a sign of resistance to Roman-backed kingship.
senones.e: The Italian Senones were defeated by Rome in 283 BCE. In Gaul Caesar had the rebel leader Acco flogged to death in 53 BCE, and the Senones joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Agedincum became Sens, later the seat of a powerful archbishop.

sexenio-democratico.t: Six turbulent years of revolution in Spain, from the fall of Isabella II through an elected king and a republic to the return of the Bourbons.
sexenio-democratico.o: In September 1868 a military rising led by Generals Juan Prim and Francisco Serrano and Admiral Juan Bautista Topete, known as the Glorious Revolution, drove Isabella II into exile. A provisional government called elections by universal male suffrage, and the Constitution of 1869 declared Spain a constitutional monarchy.
sexenio-democratico.r: With the throne vacant, Serrano acted as regent while Prim searched Europe for a king, a search that helped trigger the Franco-Prussian War. The Cortes chose Amadeo of Savoy, but Prim was assassinated in December 1870, days before he arrived. Amadeo faced Carlist rebellion, war in Cuba and fractious parties, and abdicated in February 1873.
sexenio-democratico.e: The Spanish First Republic followed, collapsing into the Pavía coup of January 1874. In December 1874 General Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII at Sagunto, opening Restoration Spain.

second-taifa-of-almeria.t: Almería's brief independence in the 1140s, ended when a Castilian, Genoese and Catalan crusade stormed the great port in 1147.
second-taifa-of-almeria.o: In 1145 the people of Almería, then the chief Andalusi port and naval base, rose against the Almoravids. Power passed to local leaders, notably the admiral Ibn Maymun, whose family had commanded the Almoravid fleet.
second-taifa-of-almeria.r: Almería remained a centre of silk weaving and Mediterranean trade, but also of corsair raiding against Christian shipping, which made it a target for Genoa and Pisa. Its new rulers had little time to establish a stable government.
second-taifa-of-almeria.e: In October 1147 Alfonso VII of Castile, with Genoese, Pisan, Catalan and Navarrese forces, captured Almería after a siege, creating Castilian Almería.

souliote-confederacy.t: Self-governing community of Orthodox warrior clans in the mountains of Epirus, famous for resisting Ali Pasha of Ioannina for over a decade.
souliote-confederacy.o: Souli was a group of villages in the rugged mountains of Thesprotia in Epirus. From the mid-17th century Orthodox Christian families, mainly Albanian-speaking, settled there and built a free community outside effective Ottoman control, growing into a confederation of villages such as Souli, Kiafa, Avariko and Samoniva.
souliote-confederacy.r: Souliote society was organised in clans (fares), each with its own leader; a council of chiefs decided on war. Men were full-time warriors who lived from herding and from tribute imposed on surrounding villages; women also fought. Leading families included the Botsaris and Tzavelas. The Souliotes spoke Albanian and Greek and were Orthodox.
souliote-confederacy.e: Ali Pasha of Ioannina attacked repeatedly from 1792 and finally forced their surrender in December 1803. Many Souliotes went to Corfu, while women reportedly threw themselves from the cliffs at Zalongo. They returned to fight in the Greek War of Independence under Markos Botsaris.

second-taifa-of-murcia.t: The kingdom of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King, who ruled eastern al-Andalus for 25 years in alliance with Christian powers against the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-murcia.o: Muhammad ibn Mardanish, of a family of Muwallad origin from the Valencia region, took power in Murcia in 1147 amid the collapse of the Almoravids, soon adding Valencia, Jaén, Dénia and other eastern towns to his domains.
second-taifa-of-murcia.r: Known to Christians as Rey Lobo, he made treaties with Castile, Barcelona, Genoa and Pisa, hired Christian mercenaries and minted gold coins widely used in Christian Iberia. He built palaces such as the Castillejo de Monteagudo near Murcia and kept a sophisticated court while fighting the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-murcia.e: After losing allies and territory, Ibn Mardanish died in 1172, and his sons submitted to the Almohads, who married into his family. Murcia later revived as the Third Taifa of Murcia.

salian-franks.t: Frankish group settled in Toxandria by Rome in 358, whose kings at Tournai founded the Merovingian dynasty.
salian-franks.o: The Salians were one of the Frankish peoples living near the lower Rhine. In 358 the Caesar Julian defeated them but allowed them to settle in Toxandria, in the modern Kempen, as allies of the Roman Empire. Over the next century they moved south-west towards the Scheldt.
salian-franks.r: Their kings served Rome as federate commanders. Around the 440s King Chlodio took Cambrai and the land up to the Somme. The Lex Salica, written down under Clovis, preserves their customary law, including the rule later used to bar women from the French throne.
salian-franks.e: Childeric I, son of Merovech, ruled from Tournai and fought for Rome on the Loire; his rich tomb, found in 1653, held a signet ring and gold bees. On his death in 481 his son Clovis began the conquests that created the Kingdom of the Franks.

santones.t: Gallic people of Saintonge on the Atlantic coast, whose land was the goal of the Helvetian migration of 58 BCE.
santones.o: The Santones lived north of the Gironde estuary, along the Charente, in the modern Charente-Maritime. Caesar records that the Helvetii planned to settle in their land, which alarmed him because it lay close to the Roman Province.
santones.r: Their coast gave them ships and seamen, which Caesar requisitioned in 56 BCE for the war against the Veneti. They struck coins in large numbers and traded salt and goods along the Atlantic.
santones.e: They joined the revolt of 52 BCE with twelve thousand men. Under Rome Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) became the first capital of Aquitania, with the Arch of Germanicus and a large amphitheatre. The region kept their name as Saintonge.

sotiates.t: Aquitanian people of the Sos district whose king Adiatuanus made a last stand against Rome with six hundred sworn companions.
sotiates.o: The Sotiates were one of the Aquitani, living around the oppidum of Sos in the modern Lot-et-Garonne, north of the Pyrenean foothills. They are known almost entirely from Caesar's account of the campaign of his legate Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
sotiates.r: Caesar describes their king Adiatuanus surrounded by six hundred soldurii, sworn companions who vowed to share their lord's fate and never survive him. Coins inscribed with the names of the Sotiates and of Adiatuanus confirm the account.
sotiates.e: Crassus defeated the Sotiates in open battle and besieged their oppidum, defeating Roman siege works with mines dug by men skilled in copper mining. After a failed sortie Adiatuanus surrendered. Their land later formed part of the Roman province of Aquitania.

swedish-pomerania.t: Baltic territory held by the Swedish crown for nearly two centuries, giving Sweden a foothold and a vote in the Holy Roman Empire.
swedish-pomerania.o: Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania in 1630 and occupied the duchy during the Thirty Years' War. When the last Pomeranian duke died in 1637, Sweden kept control, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 granted it Western Pomerania with Stettin, Stralsund and the island of Rügen, held as an imperial fief.
swedish-pomerania.r: The Swedish king sat in the Imperial Diet as Duke of Pomerania, but the territory kept its own estates and German law. Greifswald University continued as a centre of learning. Sweden lost Stettin and the lands south of the Peene to Prussia in 1720, and Stralsund became the seat of government. Serfdom was abolished in 1806 under Gustav IV Adolf.
swedish-pomerania.e: Under the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 Sweden ceded Pomerania to Denmark, which exchanged it with Prussia in 1815 for Saxe-Lauenburg and money. It became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania; Swedish influence survives in Stralsund's architecture.

second-taifa-of-badajoz.t: Badajoz under the Banu Wazir family, one of the western regimes that arose when Almoravid rule broke down in the 1140s.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.o: In 1145 members of the Banu Wazir, the family of Sidray ibn Wazir of the Taifa of Beja and Évora, took control of Badajoz as part of the revolt against the Almoravids that had begun in the Algarve.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the state was a frontier territory on the Guadiana facing the Kingdom of Portugal and the Kingdom of León, governed by a military family that switched alliances as needed.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.e: By 1150 the Banu Wazir had submitted to the Almohads, who kept Badajoz as a frontier stronghold. Alfonso IX of León took the city in 1230.

suessiones.t: Belgic people of the Aisne valley whose kings once ruled across Gaul and Britain, and who led the coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE.
suessiones.o: The Suessiones held fertile land along the Aisne, around Soissons. Caesar was told that within living memory their king Diviciacus had been the most powerful ruler in Gaul, holding sway over much of Belgic Gaul and over Britain.
suessiones.r: They shared laws and magistrates with their neighbours the Remi, and Caesar credits them with twelve fortified towns and fifty thousand warriors. Their king Galba was chosen to command the Belgic league in 57 BCE.
suessiones.e: After the league dispersed, Caesar besieged their oppidum of Noviodunum, and the Suessiones surrendered and were placed under the Remi. Under Rome their town Augusta Suessionum became Soissons, later capital of the Domain of Soissons and of Frankish kingdoms.

second-taifa-of-malaga.t: Málaga under the Zirid prince Tamim, who broke away from his brother's kingdom of Granada until the Almoravids removed both.
second-taifa-of-malaga.o: When the Zirid king Badis of Granada died in 1073, his grandsons divided his realm. Tamim ibn Buluggin received Málaga and ruled it as an independent taifa, while his brother Abd Allah held the Taifa of Granada.
second-taifa-of-malaga.r: Tamim governed a prosperous port city producing silk, ceramics and dried fruit. The brothers quarrelled and fought over border towns, and both paid tribute to Alfonso VI of Castile. Tamim joined the Almoravid campaign of 1086 but, like other taifa kings, was distrusted by their emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin.
second-taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1090 the Almoravids deposed both Tamim and Abd Allah. Tamim was exiled to the Sus in Morocco. Málaga became an Almoravid city and later re-emerged briefly as the Third Taifa of Málaga.

suebi.t: A broad grouping of Germanic peoples between the Elbe and the Rhine whose name Roman writers used for half of Germania and which later gave Swabia its name.
suebi.o: The Suebi enter history in 58 BCE when Julius Caesar fought their leader Ariovistus in Alsace, after he had crossed the Rhine about 72 BCE to aid the Sequani. Caesar describes the Suebi as the largest and most warlike people of Germania. Tacitus later used the name for a whole cluster of peoples around the Elbe, including the Semnones, Marcomanni and Quadi.
suebi.r: The Suebi were less a single state than a loose family of tribes sharing cult and customs. Tacitus describes the 'Suebian knot' hairstyle worn by free warriors and an annual sacrifice in the sacred grove of the Semnones, regarded as the oldest and noblest of the group. Leadership rested with kings or war-leaders chosen for campaigns, and their economy combined farming with cattle raising.
suebi.e: After the 3rd century the name was absorbed into new groupings, especially the Alemanni, whose land became known as Swabia. A separate Suebian group crossed the Rhine in 406 and founded a kingdom in Gallaecia in north-west Spain, which lasted until the Visigoths conquered it in 585.

salyes.t: Celto-Ligurian confederation inland of Marseille whose wars with Greek Massalia drew Rome into Gaul and led to the founding of Aix-en-Provence.
salyes.o: The Salyes were a league of Ligurian and Celtic communities in lower Provence, between the Rhône and the Var. Greek writers mention them from the 4th century BCE as troublesome neighbours of Massalia. Their chief stronghold was the oppidum of Entremont on a plateau north of modern Aix, fortified in the 2nd century BCE.
salyes.r: Entremont is known for its stone sculptures of seated warriors and carved severed heads, and for a portico where real skulls were displayed, reflecting a warrior cult of the head. The Salyes farmed olives and cereals, pressed oil and traded with the Greek coast while raiding it.
salyes.e: Massalia appealed to the Roman Republic, and campaigns in 125 to 123 BCE under Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Sextius Calvinus destroyed Entremont. Their king Teutomalius fled to the Allobroges. In 122 BCE the Romans founded Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence) nearby, and the territory became part of Gallia Narbonensis.

sicel-league.t: Short-lived union of the native Sicel towns of eastern Sicily under Ducetius, who tried to resist the Greek cities in the mid-5th century BCE.
sicel-league.o: The Sicels were the native people of eastern Sicily, gradually pushed inland by the Greek colonies. After the fall of the tyrants in Syracuse and Acragas in the 460s BCE, the Sicel leader Ducetius united most Sicel communities, apart from Hybla, around 460 BCE.
sicel-league.r: Ducetius founded new towns, including Menaenum and Palike, beside the sanctuary of the Palici, twin gods worshipped at volcanic pools that served as a place of oaths and refuge for slaves. He took Morgantina and Inessa and attacked Acragan and Syracusan territory. The league was a military federation built around his leadership.
sicel-league.e: In 450 BCE Syracuse and Acragas defeated Ducetius at Nomae; he surrendered and was exiled to Corinth. He returned to found Kale Akte on the north coast but died around 440 BCE, and Syracuse absorbed the Sicel towns. The Sicels were gradually Hellenised.

severians-balkan.t: Slavic tribe in north-eastern Bulgaria whom the Bulgars under Asparuh placed to guard the eastern passes of the Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.o: Known mainly from Byzantine chronicles, the Severi were a Slavic tribe that settled in Moesia in the 7th century, in the area between the Danube delta and the eastern Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.r: They lived as a tribal people under their own chiefs. When the Bulgars arrived under Asparuh in 680–681, Theophanes records that the Severi were moved to guard the passes towards Byzantium, while the Seven Slavic Tribes held other borders.
severians-balkan.e: They became part of the First Bulgarian Empire, keeping their own leaders for some time; in the 760s the Byzantine emperor Constantine V captured Slavun, chief of the Severi. They then merged into the Bulgarian population.

smyrna.t: Ancient Greek city on the Gulf of Izmir, a claimed birthplace of Homer, destroyed by Lydia and refounded in the Hellenistic age.
smyrna.o: Old Smyrna, at Bayraklı on the Gulf of Izmir, was settled by Aeolian Greeks c. 1000 BCE and taken over by Ionian exiles from Colophon, probably in the 8th century BCE. It developed into one of the first Greek cities with planned streets and stone walls, and claimed to be the birthplace of Homer.
smyrna.r: The city prospered from the fertile Hermus plain. Its temple of Athena is among the earliest monumental Ionian sanctuaries. It was not one of the original twelve members of the Ionian League. Smyrna fought the Kingdom of Lydia, resisting Gyges, but Alyattes destroyed it c. 600 BCE, after which it survived only as villages.
smyrna.e: Antigonus and Lysimachus refounded Smyrna on the slopes of Mount Pagus c. 300 BCE, and it joined the Ionian League. It sided with Rome against Antiochus III and passed into the province of Asia after 133 BCE, growing into the modern city of Izmir.

saguntum.t: The Iberian town of Arse, Rome's ally, whose siege and destruction by Hannibal in 219 BCE started the Second Punic War.
saguntum.o: Saguntum, called Arse by its inhabitants, grew in the 5th century BCE on a long rocky hill above the Palancia river, near the coast north of Valencia, within the Edetanian world. Greek writers wrongly believed it had been founded by settlers from Zakynthos.
saguntum.r: It was a prosperous Iberian town trading by sea with Greeks and Phoenicians and minting silver coins with the legend Arse. In the 220s BCE it made an alliance with Rome, though it lay south of the Ebro, the limit agreed between Rome and Hasdrubal in 226 BCE.
saguntum.e: In 219 BCE Hannibal besieged Saguntum for eight months and took it, and Rome's declaration of war on Carthage followed. The Scipios recaptured the town in 212 BCE and restored its people. Saguntum flourished as a Roman municipium, whose theatre and walls still survive.

second-taifa-of-mertola.t: A Sufi-led rebel state in the Algarve whose leader Ibn Qasi rose against the Almoravids and opened the way for the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-mertola.o: Ibn Qasi, a former tax official turned Sufi teacher, gathered disciples called the Muridun in the western Algarve. In 1144, as Almoravid rule weakened, his followers seized Mértola, and he proclaimed himself imam and mahdi.
second-taifa-of-mertola.r: The movement combined religious reform with rebellion against Almoravid taxes and jurists. Ibn Qasi was allied for a time with Ibn al-Mundhir of Silves and Sidray ibn Wazir of Beja, but they soon turned against him. He was among the first to appeal to the Almohads in Morocco, then sought support from Afonso I of Portugal.
second-taifa-of-mertola.e: His alliance with Portugal angered his own supporters, who killed him in Silves in 1151. Mértola passed to the Almohads, and his mystical writings were later studied by Ibn Arabi.

siphnos.t: Cycladic island that grew briefly rich on gold and silver mines and built a celebrated treasury at Delphi.
siphnos.o: Siphnos, in the western Cyclades, was settled by Ionian Greeks from Athens in the early Iron Age. Its silver and gold deposits, worked since the Bronze Age, made it in the 6th century BCE the richest island of the Aegean, according to Herodotus.
siphnos.r: Siphnians shared their mining income as citizens and gave a tithe to Delphi, where they built the Siphnian Treasury c. 525 BCE, with its famous sculpted frieze. Exiles from Samos extorted a hundred talents from the island c. 524 BCE. Siphnos later sent a ship to Salamis and paid tribute in the Delian League.
siphnos.e: The mines failed, flooded by the sea, which legend blamed on the Siphnians cheating Apollo of his tithe. The island remained a modest community known for its pottery under Hellenistic powers and Rome, losing independence by 146 BCE.

second-french-empire.t: Napoleon III's empire, which rebuilt Paris, built railways and a colonial empire, and collapsed after defeat by Prussia at Sedan in 1870.
second-french-empire.o: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president of the French Second Republic, seized dictatorial power in a coup in December 1851. A plebiscite approved restoring the empire, and on 2 December 1852 he became Emperor Napoleon III.
second-french-empire.r: The early empire was authoritarian, with censorship and managed elections. Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris with boulevards and sewers, and railways, banks and department stores expanded. France fought in the Crimea, helped unify Italy and gained Nice and Savoy in 1860, but the Mexican intervention failed. From 1860 the regime liberalised, becoming a parliamentary 'Liberal Empire' under Émile Ollivier in 1870.
second-french-empire.e: Provoked by Bismarck, France declared war on Prussia in July 1870. Napoleon III was captured at Sedan on 2 September, and two days later the French Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. He died in exile in England in 1873.

sidicini.t: Small Oscan people of northern Campania whose appeal for help against the Samnites in 343 BCE set off Rome's first war with Samnium.
sidicini.o: The Sidicini lived around Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano) in the hills between the Roccamonfina volcano and the Volturno, bordering the Aurunci and Campanians. They were an Oscan-speaking people, possibly related to the Samnites or the Ausones; their earlier history is unknown.
sidicini.r: Known mainly from Livy, they formed a small community centred on Teanum, which later issued its own coins in Oscan. In 343 BCE the Samnites attacked them; the Sidicini sought help from Capua, and Capua's appeal to Rome began the First Samnite War. They joined the Latins and Campanians against Rome in 340 BCE.
sidicini.e: Rome founded the Latin colony of Cales on land taken from the Sidicini and Aurunci in 334 BCE, ending their independence. Teanum Sidicinum became a Roman ally and later a municipium and colony.

samnite-league.t: Confederation of the Oscan-speaking peoples of the southern Apennines, Rome's toughest opponent in Italy during three Samnite Wars.
samnite-league.o: The Samnites lived in the mountains of modern Molise and inland Campania. They believed they descended from Sabines who had migrated south in a 'sacred spring'. By the 5th century BCE they had formed a confederation of four peoples, the Pentri, Caraceni, Caudini and Hirpini, with Bovianum as a main centre.
samnite-league.r: Each people (touto) was governed by an elected magistrate, the meddix tuticus, and the league acted together in war. Society was rural, living in villages and hill forts. The great sanctuary at Pietrabbondante, with its temple and theatre, was a federal centre. Samnite warriors were famed for their armour, and their expansion carried Oscan speech into Campania, Lucania and Bruttium.
samnite-league.e: Rome fought three Samnite Wars from 343 to 290 BCE. The Samnites trapped a Roman army at the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE but lost at Sentinum in 295 BCE and accepted Roman alliance in 290 BCE. They later backed Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and Sulla crushed them at the Colline Gate in 82 BCE.

second-taifa-of-niebla.t: Niebla's brief independence under Yusuf al-Bitruji during the 1140s revolts against the Almoravids in the far west of al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-niebla.o: In 1145 Yusuf ibn Ahmad al-Bitruji, a local leader, took control of the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, as the revolt begun by Ibn Qasi in the Algarve spread through the south-west.
second-taifa-of-niebla.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Niebla was one of several small regimes that rose and fell in quick succession. Its ruler was drawn into conflicts with Almoravid loyalists in Seville and with neighbouring rebels.
second-taifa-of-niebla.e: Niebla submitted to the Almohads around 1150. A century later it became independent again as the Third Taifa of Niebla.

sugambri.t: A warlike Germanic people of the lower Rhine who repeatedly defied Rome until Augustus deported much of the tribe across the river into Gaul.
sugambri.o: The Sugambri lived on the east bank of the Rhine between the Sieg and the Lippe. They first appear in 55 BCE, when they sheltered survivors of the Usipetes and Tencteri; Julius Caesar bridged the Rhine and ravaged their land in retaliation.
sugambri.r: Little is known of their internal organisation beyond war-leaders and a reputation for raiding. In 16 BCE they crossed the Rhine with the Usipetes and Tencteri and defeated the Roman legate Marcus Lollius, capturing the eagle of the Fifth Legion, an event known as the clades Lolliana. This defeat helped prompt Augustus' German campaigns.
sugambri.e: Drusus attacked them from 12 BCE, and in 8 BCE Tiberius forcibly resettled tens of thousands on the left bank of the Rhine, where they became the Cugerni. Those who stayed merged into later groups, and the name was later absorbed into the Frankish confederation; Frankish kings were poetically called Sicambri.

silvanectes.t: Small Gallic people of the forests north of Paris whose town Augustomagus became Senlis.
silvanectes.o: The Silvanectes are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the Suessiones during the conquest. Pliny and Ptolemy record them as a separate people between the Parisii, Bellovaci and Suessiones.
silvanectes.r: Their name has been linked to the forests of the Oise, but nothing is recorded of their society.
silvanectes.e: Under Rome they formed a civitas with Augustomagus (Senlis) as its chief town. It became a bishopric and in 987 the assembly at Senlis elected Hugh Capet king, founding the Kingdom of France.

sestos.t: Greek city on the European shore of the Hellespont, key to the grain route, whose capture by Athens in 478 BCE closes Herodotus's Histories.
sestos.o: Sestos was founded by Aeolian settlers from Lesbos on the Thracian Chersonese, at the narrows of the Hellespont opposite Abydos. Its harbour and position made it the main crossing point from Asia into Europe.
sestos.r: Sestos lay near the site of Xerxes's bridges in 480 BCE. In 479 to 478 BCE the Athenians under Xanthippus besieged and took it, the episode that ends Herodotus's Histories. It became a key Athenian base for protecting the Black Sea grain route and paid tribute in the Delian League. Greek legend made it the home of Hero, beloved of Leander.
sestos.e: After the Athenian defeat at nearby Aegospotami in 405 BCE, Sestos passed to Sparta, then back to Athens and later to Macedonian and Hellenistic rulers. It came under Roman control by 146 BCE.

sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.t: A Republican regional government in Asturias that declared itself sovereign when cut off from the rest of Republican Spain in 1937.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.o: After Bilbao and Santander fell to Franco in the summer of 1937, Asturias and part of León were isolated from the Republican government in Valencia. On 24 August 1937 the Interprovincial Council at Gijón, led by the Socialist miners' leader Belarmino Tomás, declared itself sovereign.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.r: The council took over all civil and military powers, issued its own decrees and money, and tried to organise defence of the mountains and the mining valleys with exhausted troops and few supplies. The central government saw the declaration as a step too far, but could do little.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.e: Nationalist forces broke through in October 1937. Leaders and soldiers fled by sea, and Franco's troops entered Gijón on 21 October 1937, ending the war in the north.

sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.t: The transitional Dutch state of 1813–1815, created as Napoleon's empire collapsed, under the returning Prince of Orange as sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.o: After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, French authority in the Netherlands collapsed in November 1813. A provisional government led by Gijsbert Karel van Hogendorp invited William Frederick, son of the last stadtholder, to return. He landed at Scheveningen on 30 November and accepted the title of sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.r: William ruled under a new constitution adopted in 1814, which gave the sovereign wide powers while keeping a States General. The new state rejected the old federal republic in favour of the unitary government created in the Batavian period. Its priority was rebuilding finances and securing allied backing at the Congress of Vienna.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.e: The great powers decided to unite the northern and southern Netherlands as a barrier to France. In March 1815, during Napoleon's Hundred Days, William proclaimed himself king, creating the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

spanish-netherlands.t: The southern Low Countries under the Spanish Habsburgs, battleground of Europe and home of Rubens, which survived the Dutch Revolt but lost land to France.
spanish-netherlands.o: In 1555–1556 Charles V passed the Habsburg Netherlands to his son Philip II of Spain. Philip's persecution of Protestants, new bishoprics and taxes provoked the Dutch Revolt from 1566. After the Duke of Alba's harsh rule, the southern provinces made peace with Philip through the Union of Arras in 1579.
spanish-netherlands.r: The Duke of Parma reconquered Flanders and Brabant, taking Antwerp in 1585, while the north became the Dutch Republic. The Archdukes Albert and Isabella governed from 1598 to 1621 and agreed the Twelve Years' Truce. The provinces became a Counter-Reformation stronghold; Rubens worked in Antwerp. The Treaty of Münster of 1648 closed the Scheldt, hurting Antwerp's trade.
spanish-netherlands.e: Louis XIV took Artois, Lille, Cambrai and other lands between 1659 and 1678. After the War of the Spanish Succession, the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt in 1713–1714 gave the territory to Austria as the Austrian Netherlands.

segontiaci.t: British people recorded only by Julius Caesar, one of five groups that submitted to him in 54 BCE during his second campaign in Britain.
segontiaci.o: The Segontiaci appear once in Caesar's Gallic War, among the peoples who surrendered after the Trinovantes made terms with Rome in 54 BCE. The others were the Cenimagni, Ancalites, Bibroci and Cassi.
segontiaci.r: Nothing is known of their government or way of life. Their territory has often been placed in northern Hampshire, around the later Roman town of Calleva, partly because a Roman-period name there has been compared with theirs, but this remains a guess.
segontiaci.e: They disappear from the record after 54 BCE. If they lived around Silchester, their lands were later part of the realm of the Atrebates (Britain) before the Roman conquest of 43.

sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.t: The independent Sicily proclaimed in the revolution of 1848, which deposed the Bourbons and held out for sixteen months.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.o: On 12 January 1848 Palermo rose against Ferdinand II of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, one of the first revolutions of that year in Europe. The rebels took most of the island, revived the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and formed a government under the veteran admiral Ruggero Settimo.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.r: The Sicilian parliament declared the Bourbon dynasty deposed in April 1848 and in July offered the crown to Ferdinando, Duke of Genoa, son of Charles Albert of the Kingdom of Sardinia, who declined. The state had a government, parliament and army, but was divided between moderates and radicals and lacked foreign support.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.e: Ferdinand II's troops bombarded and took Messina in September 1848. The Bourbon offensive resumed in 1849, Catania fell in April and Palermo surrendered in May 1849, ending the kingdom.

sorbs.t: West Slavic tribes between the Saale and the Bóbr whose descendants, the Sorbs of Lusatia, are still a recognised minority in Germany.
sorbs.o: Slavic groups settled the lands east of the Saale and Elbe in the 6th and 7th centuries. The Chronicle of Fredegar records that in 631 the Sorb prince Dervan left Frankish allegiance and joined Samo's Empire. Their territory included the regions later called Daleminzia, Milzenland (Upper Lusatia) and Lusatia.
sorbs.r: The Sorbs were organised in small tribal territories, each centred on fortified strongholds (gords) such as those at Tornow and Raddusch, with no lasting central ruler. They farmed, raised livestock and worshipped Slavic gods. Frankish sources record frequent wars and tribute payments, and Charlemagne's Limes Sorabicus marked the boundary with them.
sorbs.e: East Francia's king Henry the Fowler took the Daleminzian stronghold of Gana in 929 and founded Meissen. By 932 the Sorbian tribes were tributary, and the Marca Geronis and later the Margraviate of Meissen and Lusatia absorbed them. Sorbs survive today in Lusatia, keeping their language.

sexi.t: A Phoenician colony at Almuñécar on Spain's southern coast, known for its rich tombs and for salted fish exported across the Mediterranean.
sexi.o: Sexi was founded by Phoenicians in the 8th century BCE on the headland of modern Almuñécar, in Granada province. It formed part of the string of Phoenician harbours along the Andalusian coast, between Malaka and Abdera.
sexi.r: Its Laurita necropolis has yielded Egyptian alabaster vases reused as burial urns, evidence of the colonists' wide contacts. The city's economy rested on trade and on fish salting, and its later Punic-legend coins carried tuna, the source of its wealth. Its government is not recorded.
sexi.e: With the Roman conquest of the south after 206 BCE, Sexi passed under Roman control. It kept its fish-salting industry and became the Roman town of Firmum Iulium Sexi, ancestor of modern Almuñécar.

samos.t: Ionian island state that under the tyrant Polycrates became the leading naval power of the Aegean and built the famous Tunnel of Eupalinos.
samos.o: Ionian settlers occupied Samos, opposite Mount Mycale, c. 1000 BCE, beside an older cult of Hera at the Heraion. Samos joined the Ionian League and by the 7th century BCE was a seafaring state: the Samian Colaeus reached Tartessos in Spain, and the city founded colonies such as Perinthus.
samos.r: Polycrates seized power c. 538 BCE and built a fleet of a hundred ships, a harbour mole, the 1,036 metre aqueduct tunnel of Eupalinos and a vast new temple of Hera. Pythagoras left to escape his rule. Samos was later a privileged ship-providing member of the Delian League, birthplace of Aristarchus and Epicurus.
samos.e: Pericles crushed a Samian revolt in 440 to 439 BCE, and Athenian settlers held the island from 365 to 322 BCE. Samos then served as a Ptolemaic naval base before passing under Pergamene and finally Roman control, becoming part of the province of Asia in 129 BCE.

smertae.t: People of the interior of Sutherland in northern Scotland, named only in Ptolemy's Geography.
smertae.o: The Smertae are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them inland in the far north of Scotland, usually located in central Sutherland around the upper Oykel and Shin valleys. Their name may be linked to the Celtic god Smertrios, or to a word meaning 'smeared', perhaps referring to body paint.
smertae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. The interior of Sutherland was a land of moorland and river valleys, with scattered roundhouses and brochs along the straths, and the population lived mainly by herding cattle and sheep and growing small crops of barley.
smertae.e: The Smertae are not mentioned again. Their region later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts and, from the 9th century, came under Norse influence as the name Sutherland, the 'southern land' of the Norse earls, shows.

saxons.t: A confederation of north German peoples who raided Roman coasts, settled England and fought Charlemagne for thirty years before forced conversion.
saxons.o: The Saxons are named by Ptolemy in the 2nd century and appear as sea raiders on the coasts of Gaul and Britain from the late 3rd century. They absorbed older peoples such as the Chauci, Angrivarii and Cherusci, spreading from Holstein across the plains between the Elbe and the Rhine. From the 5th century many settled in Britain.
saxons.r: Continental Saxony had no king. Bede records that it was ruled by many satraps, and later sources describe an assembly at Marklo where representatives of nobles, freemen and freedmen from Westphalia, Engern and Eastphalia met. Their sacred places included the Irminsul, a great pillar or tree.
saxons.e: Charlemagne attacked Saxony in 772, destroying the Irminsul. The Saxon Wars, with the resistance of Widukind and the massacre at Verden in 782, ended with deportations in 804. Saxony was baptised and incorporated into the Frankish realm, later forming the Duchy of Saxony, whose dukes became East Francia's kings in 919.

sparta.t: Militarised city-state of Laconia with two kings and a helot workforce, the dominant land power of Classical Greece and victor over Athens in 404 BCE.
sparta.o: Dorian Greeks settled the Eurotas valley in Laconia in the 10th century BCE, and four villages joined to form Sparta, later absorbing nearby Amyclae. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Sparta conquered Messenia, reducing its people to helots, state serfs who farmed the land for Spartan citizens.
sparta.r: Sparta had two hereditary kings, from the Agiad and Eurypontid houses, a council of elders, five annual ephors and an assembly, a system credited to the lawgiver Lycurgus. Male citizens underwent the agoge training and lived in messes. Sparta led the Peloponnesian League and the Hellenic Alliance against Persia, where Leonidas I fell at Thermopylae in 480 BCE.
sparta.e: Sparta defeated Athens in 404 BCE, but Thebes broke its power at Leuctra in 371 BCE and freed Messenia. The reformer Cleomenes III was defeated in 222 BCE. Sparta was forced into the Achaean League in 192 BCE and came under Rome in 146 BCE as a free city.

second-taifa-of-silves.t: Silves under the rebel Ibn al-Mundhir, one of the Algarve leaders who rose with Ibn Qasi against the Almoravids in 1144.
second-taifa-of-silves.o: In 1144 Abu Muhammad ibn al-Mundhir, a local notable and disciple of the Sufi leader Ibn Qasi, took Silves during the uprising of the Muridun against the Almoravids and governed it as an independent lord.
second-taifa-of-silves.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Ibn al-Mundhir's rule was one of the short-lived regimes of the second taifa period. He first backed Ibn Qasi of the Second Taifa of Mértola, then joined Sidray ibn Wazir of Beja against him.
second-taifa-of-silves.e: Around 1150 Silves accepted Almohad authority. Ibn Qasi was killed in the city in 1151. Silves was taken briefly by Sancho I of Portugal in 1189, lost again, and finally conquered by Portugal in 1242.

selonians.t: Small Baltic people on the south bank of the Daugava, the first of the Latvian tribes to fall to the German crusaders in 1208.
selonians.o: The Selonians settled in what is now south-eastern Latvia and north-eastern Lithuania during the first millennium, between the Semigallians and the Latgalians. Their name survives in the region of Sēlija. They lived in communities centred on hillforts, without a single ruler.
selonians.r: Archaeology shows farming villages, fortified hills and graves rich in bronze ornaments. Their position on the Daugava trade route brought them under the influence of Polotsk and, by the 12th century, of the Lithuanians, who used their main fortress, Sēlpils, as a base for raids.
selonians.e: In 1208 Bishop Albert of Riga and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword besieged and took Sēlpils, and the Selonians accepted baptism. Their land was later divided between the Livonian Order and the Archbishopric of Riga, and a short-lived Bishopric of Selonia was founded. The Selonians merged into the Latvian and Lithuanian peoples.

segusiavi.t: Gallic people of the Forez and Lyonnais on whose land Rome founded Lyon, the future capital of the Three Gauls.
segusiavi.o: The Segusiavi lived between the Loire and the Rhône, in the plains of the Forez and the hills west of the Saône. Caesar describes them as the first people beyond the Rhône outside the Roman Province and as clients of the Aedui.
segusiavi.r: Few details survive. Their territory commanded the crossing of the Saône and Rhône at the hill of Fourvière, a strategic point for trade between the Mediterranean and central Gaul.
segusiavi.e: They joined the revolt of 52 BCE with the Aedui. In 43 BCE the colony of Lugdunum (Lyon) was founded on their land, and their own chief town became Forum Segusiavorum (Feurs). Their name survives in the Forez region.

silures.t: Warlike people of south-east Wales who resisted Rome for nearly thirty years, until legions at Caerleon held their land and Caerwent became their town.
silures.o: The Silures lived in the valleys and coastal plain of Glamorgan and Gwent, defended by hillforts such as Llanmelin. Tacitus, noting their dark complexions and curly hair, speculated that they had come from Spain, a guess no longer accepted. They first appear in 47, when Rome began its advance into Wales.
silures.r: Little is known of their leadership; they seem to have been a confederation of communities rather than a single kingdom, without a coinage of their own. Their warfare relied on raids and ambush in difficult country. Caratacus fought alongside them after 47, and in 52 they defeated a legion under Manlius Valens; the governor Ostorius Scapula died worn out by the campaign.
silures.e: Julius Frontinus finally subdued them around 74 to 78 and founded the legionary fortress of Isca at Caerleon. Their territory became a civitas within Roman Britain with its centre at Venta Silurum, Caerwent, where an inscription records the council of the Silures. The later Kingdom of Gwent grew in the same region.

semigallians.t: Baltic people of the fertile Lielupe plain who fought the Livonian crusaders longer than any other, finally abandoning their land in 1290.
semigallians.o: The Semigallians settled the plain of the Lielupe river in central Latvia and northern Lithuania in the first millennium. By the 12th century they had a network of strong hillforts, with Tērvete and Mežotne among the most important, and their land was the granary of the region.
semigallians.r: Regional leaders sometimes acted together under a single war chief. Viesturs allied with the Germans of Riga against the Lithuanians early in the 13th century, then turned against them and joined the Lithuanian victory over the Livonian Brothers of the Sword at Saule in 1236. Trade along the Daugava and Lielupe brought them silver and connections with Rus'.
semigallians.e: The Livonian Order fought them through the 1270s and 1280s; Nameisis led a major revolt. In 1290 the last Semigallians burned their hillforts and many moved south into Lithuania. Their land was divided between the Order and the Archbishopric of Riga, and Zemgale remains a region of Latvia.

suessetani.t: A little-known people of the Cinco Villas region of Aragon, whose town Corbio fell to Rome in 184 BCE.
suessetani.o: The Suessetani lived north of the middle Ebro, probably in the Cinco Villas area of modern Aragon, between the Sedetani and the Vascones. Their origins and language are uncertain; some scholars think they were of Celtic rather than Iberian stock. They appear only in Livy's account of the Roman wars.
suessetani.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their main town, Corbio. They joined the Ilergetes in raids and in the anti-Roman revolts of the early 2nd century BCE.
suessetani.e: In 184 BCE the Roman praetor Aulus Terentius Varro captured Corbio and sold its inhabitants into slavery. The Suessetani disappear from history soon afterwards, and their lands seem to have passed to neighbouring peoples, possibly the Vascones.

sinope.t: Milesian colony with the best harbour on the southern Black Sea, birthplace of Diogenes the Cynic and later capital of the Kingdom of Pontus.
sinope.o: Miletus founded Sinope on a peninsula on the north coast of Anatolia; ancient sources give dates in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, and the register follows c. 631 BCE. Its sheltered harbour made it the main Greek port of the southern Black Sea.
sinope.r: Sinope founded colonies of its own, including Trapezus, Cerasus and Cotyora, and traded tuna, timber and red ochre called Sinopic earth. It was under the Achaemenid Empire and later independent. Pericles's Black Sea expedition of c. 437 BCE installed Athenian settlers. Diogenes the Cynic was born there c. 412 BCE.
sinope.e: Pharnaces I of the Kingdom of Pontus captured Sinope in 183 BCE and made it his capital; Mithridates VI was born there. Rome took it in 70 BCE. It is the modern Turkish town of Sinop.

state-of-the-presidi.t: A string of Spanish-held fortresses on the Tuscan coast that let Spain and later Naples watch over central Italy for nearly 250 years.
state-of-the-presidi.o: When Philip II of Spain granted the conquered Republic of Siena to Cosimo I de' Medici in 1557, he kept the coastal fortresses of Orbetello, Porto Ercole, Talamone, Porto Santo Stefano and Ansedonia. Porto Longone on Elba was added in 1603.
state-of-the-presidi.r: The Presidi, meaning garrisons, were run as a military district under the viceroy of the Kingdom of Naples. Their purpose was strategic: to secure Spanish sea routes between Naples, Genoa and Barcelona and to watch the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Spain built powerful fortifications at Porto Ercole and Orbetello. The painter Caravaggio died at Porto Ercole in 1610.
state-of-the-presidi.e: The Presidi passed with Naples to Austria in 1707 and to the Bourbons in 1735. In 1801 the Treaty of Florence ceded them to France, which joined them to the Kingdom of Etruria; after 1815 they became part of Tuscany.

second-spanish-republic.t: Spain's democratic republic of the 1930s, whose sweeping reforms and deep divisions ended in civil war and Franco's dictatorship.
second-spanish-republic.o: After republican parties won the cities in the municipal elections of 12 April 1931, Alfonso XIII left Spain and the republic was proclaimed on 14 April, ending Restoration Spain. The Constitution of December 1931 created a secular, democratic state with women's suffrage.
second-spanish-republic.r: Governments led by Manuel Azaña pursued land reform, army reform, separation of Church and state and Catalan autonomy. A centre-right coalition reversed many reforms after 1933, and the Asturian miners' revolution of 1934 was crushed. The Popular Front won the elections of February 1936 amid rising political violence.
second-spanish-republic.e: A military coup on 17-18 July 1936 began the Spanish Civil War. The Republic, aided by the Soviet Union and the International Brigades, lost to Franco's Nationalists. Madrid fell in March 1939, and the war ended on 1 April, giving way to Francoist Spain.

sudovians.t: Warlike West Baltic people of the lake and forest country between the Neman and Narew, who held off Rus', Poland and the Teutonic Order for centuries.
sudovians.o: Ptolemy's 'Sudinoi' in the 2nd century are usually taken to be the Sudovians, also called Yotvingians. They occupied the lands around modern Suwałki, Grodno and southern Lithuania, close kin of the Prussians and Galindians, and were organised as a loose federation of territories led by hillfort chieftains rather than a single state.
sudovians.r: Their economy rested on farming, cattle, hunting and the amber and fur trade, supplemented by raiding. They kept Baltic pagan cults and a language close to Old Prussian. Rus' princes campaigned against them from Vladimir the Great's expedition of 983, and Polish dukes repeatedly invaded in the 12th and 13th centuries; Bolesław V the Chaste killed the chief Komata in 1264.
sudovians.e: After 1274 the Teutonic Order turned on Sudovia, and in 1283 its last war leader, Skomantas, submitted. Many Sudovians were resettled in Sambia, in a district long called the Sudauer Winkel, while others fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The emptied land became a frontier wilderness, and the language died out.

segovellauni.t: Small Gallic people of the middle Rhône valley around Valence, absorbed into Rome's first province in Gaul.
segovellauni.o: Known only from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Segovellauni lived on the left bank of the Rhône around modern Valence, between the Allobroges to the north and the Cavares to the south. They may have been dependents of the Allobroges or the Cavares.
segovellauni.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or society beyond their position on the Rhône corridor, the main route between the Mediterranean and central Gaul.
segovellauni.e: Their land passed under Roman control after the victories over the Allobroges and Arverni in 121 BCE. The Roman colony of Valentia (Valence) was founded in their territory, probably under Caesar or Augustus.

segesta.t: Chief city of the Elymians of western Sicily, whose rivalry with Selinous drew both Athens and Carthage into Sicily.
segesta.o: Segesta was the main town of the Elymians, a people of north-western Sicily who claimed Trojan descent; Thucydides says they were Trojan refugees joined by Phocians. The city grew on Monte Barbaro in the 7th century BCE and became increasingly Hellenised while keeping close ties with the Phoenicians of Motya and Panormus.
segesta.r: Segesta minted coins with Greek legends and wrote its own Elymian language in Greek letters, known from short inscriptions. Its unfinished Doric temple of the late 5th century BCE and its hilltop theatre are among the best-preserved Greek monuments in Sicily. Its long border dispute with Selinous led it to seek Athenian help in 416 BCE, prompting the Sicilian Expedition, and then Carthaginian help, which ended in the destruction of Selinous in 409 BCE.
segesta.e: Agathocles of Syracuse massacred many citizens in 307 BCE. In the First Punic War Segesta went over to Rome, citing shared Trojan ancestry, and after 241 BCE it was a privileged free town of Roman Sicily. It was abandoned in the Middle Ages.

serbian-despotate.t: Last medieval Serbian state, which held out against the Ottomans for half a century from its fortresses on the Danube and its rich silver mines.
serbian-despotate.o: After the battle of Kosovo in 1389, Lazar's son Stefan Lazarević ruled Moravian Serbia as an Ottoman vassal. Following the Ottoman defeat at Ankara in 1402, the Byzantine emperor granted him the title of despot, and he made Belgrade his capital with Hungarian backing. In 1427 the despotate passed to his nephew Đurađ Branković.
serbian-despotate.r: The despotate drew great wealth from the silver mines of Novo Brdo and Srebrenica, worked partly by Saxon miners and traded through Ragusa. Stefan Lazarević was a writer and patron, and the Resava school of scribes refined Serbian Church Slavonic. When Belgrade returned to Hungary, Đurađ built the vast fortress of Smederevo on the Danube between 1428 and 1430.
serbian-despotate.e: The Ottomans overran Serbia in 1439, but the Peace of Szeged restored Đurađ in 1444. After his death in 1456 and that of his son Lazar in 1458, internal quarrels left Smederevo exposed, and Mehmed II took it in 1459, ending Serbian independence until the 19th century.

sicyon.t: City of the northern Peloponnese ruled by Greece's longest tyranny, a famed centre of painting and sculpture and the home of Aratus, leader of the Achaean League.
sicyon.o: Sicyon lay in a fertile plain west of Corinth, near the Gulf of Corinth. It was settled by Dorians from Argos in the early Iron Age and became an independent city. In the 7th century BCE it fell under the Orthagorid tyrants, whose rule Aristotle called the longest-lasting in Greece.
sicyon.r: The tyrant Cleisthenes, early 6th century BCE, renamed the Dorian tribes, fought Argos and helped win the First Sacred War; his daughter Agariste married into the Athenian Alcmaeonids. Sicyon was later an oligarchy and a member of the Peloponnesian League. It became famous for bronze sculpture, especially Lysippus, and for its school of painting, where Apelles studied.
sicyon.e: Demetrius Poliorcetes moved the city to a defensible plateau in 303 BCE. Aratus freed Sicyon from tyranny in 251 BCE and joined it to the Achaean League, which he then led. Sicyon passed under Rome in 146 BCE, gaining from the destruction of Corinth.

spanish-first-republic.t: Spain's first republic, which went through four presidents in eleven months amid Carlist war, cantonal revolts and war in Cuba.
spanish-first-republic.o: When Amadeo I abdicated on 11 February 1873, the Cortes proclaimed a republic, ending the monarchy of the Sexenio Democrático. Estanislao Figueras became the first head of the executive.
spanish-first-republic.r: The Republic was divided between unitary and federal republicans. Francesc Pi i Margall drafted a federal constitution dividing Spain into states, but it was never adopted. The government faced the Third Carlist War, the Cuban Ten Years' War and the Cantonal Rebellion, and its presidents, Figueras, Pi, Nicolás Salmerón and Emilio Castelar, followed in quick succession.
spanish-first-republic.e: On 3 January 1874 General Manuel Pavía dissolved the Cortes. A unitary republic under Serrano followed until General Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII in December 1874, beginning Restoration Spain.

sark.t: A tiny Channel Island fief, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which kept a feudal constitution under its Seigneur until the 21st century.
sark.o: Sark was virtually empty after the 15th century due to pirates. In 1565 Elizabeth I granted it as a fief to Helier de Carteret of Jersey, on condition that he settle it with at least forty men to defend it. He divided it into forty tenements, whose holders formed its parliament, the Chief Pleas.
sark.r: Sark was governed by its Seigneur and the Chief Pleas under Norman feudal law. Cars are banned, and the island lived from farming, fishing and later tourism. Dame Sibyl Hathaway, Dame of Sark from 1927 to 1974, led the island through German occupation from 1940 to 1945.
sark.e: In 2008 Sark held its first fully democratic elections, ending its feudal constitution. It remains a self-governing part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey and a Crown Dependency.

syracuse.t: The greatest Greek city of the West, which defeated Carthage and Athens, ruled much of Sicily under its tyrants and kings, and fell to Rome in 212 BCE.
syracuse.o: Corinthian colonists led by Archias founded Syracuse in 734 or 733 BCE on the island of Ortygia, with its freshwater spring of Arethusa and two harbours. The city expanded onto the mainland and founded daughter colonies including Kamarina, controlling south-eastern Sicily.
syracuse.r: Its politics swung between aristocracy, democracy and powerful tyrants. Gelon made it the leading Greek power and with Theron of Acragas crushed Carthage at Himera in 480 BCE. A democracy defeated the Athenian expedition in 415–413 BCE. Dionysius I built the Epipolae walls and an empire over Sicily and southern Italy; Agathocles later took the title of king. Under Hieron II, Rome's ally from 263 BCE, Syracuse enjoyed peace and Archimedes worked there.
syracuse.e: After Hieron II's death Syracuse sided with Carthage. Marcus Claudius Marcellus besieged it from 214 BCE and took it in 212 BCE, when Archimedes was killed. It became the seat of the Roman governor of Sicily and remained a major city; its ancient centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

southern-ireland.t: The home-rule jurisdiction created by the Government of Ireland Act 1920 for twenty-six counties, which existed largely on paper until replaced by the Irish Free State.
southern-ireland.o: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 divided Ireland into two home-rule areas, Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland, each with its own Parliament under Westminster. Southern Ireland came into existence in May 1921, when elections were held for its House of Commons.
southern-ireland.r: Sinn Fein won 124 of the 128 seats unopposed but treated the election as one for the second Dail of the Irish Republic, so the Parliament of Southern Ireland met only twice, in June 1921 and January 1922. Only the four members for Dublin University attended the first meeting.
southern-ireland.e: Its second meeting approved the Anglo-Irish Treaty and set up the Provisional Government under Michael Collins. Southern Ireland was replaced by the Irish Free State on 6 December 1922.

samos-empire.t: The first known Slavic political union, led by the Frankish merchant Samo, which threw off Avar rule and defeated a Frankish king.
samos-empire.o: Around 623 the Slavs of central Europe, called Wends in the Chronicle of Fredegar, rebelled against their Avar overlords. Samo, a Frankish merchant trading with them, fought so well that they chose him as king. The location of his realm is debated, but it probably covered Bohemia, Moravia, parts of Slovakia and Lower Austria.
samos-empire.r: Fredegar, the only substantial source, reports that Samo ruled for 35 years, had twelve Slavic wives and won every battle against the Avars. In 631 a dispute over murdered Frankish merchants led King Dagobert I to invade; Samo defeated the Franks at Wogastisburg, and the Sorb prince Dervan then joined him.
samos-empire.e: After Samo's death around 658 his union seems to have dissolved, and nothing more is heard of it; the Avars regained influence in the region. It is remembered as a forerunner of later Slavic states such as Great Moravia and Carantania, though no direct continuity is known.

scordisci.t: Celtic people at the meeting of the Sava and Danube who founded Singidunum, modern Belgrade, and harried Roman Macedonia for two centuries.
scordisci.o: After the Celtic invasion of Greece under Brennus failed in 279 BCE, survivors settled at the confluence of the Sava and Danube. There they merged with local Illyrian and Thracian peoples and formed the Scordisci, with strongholds at Singidunum (Belgrade) and Taurunum (Zemun).
scordisci.r: A warrior aristocracy ruled over a mixed population, dominating the middle Danube from fortified oppida. They minted coins, traded along the river and raided south. In 114 BCE they destroyed a Roman army under Gaius Porcius Cato in Macedonia, and wars with Rome followed for decades. The Dacian king Burebista defeated them in the mid-1st century BCE.
scordisci.e: Tiberius subdued the Scordisci during his Pannonian campaigns of 12–9 BCE, and they became allies of Rome. By the early 1st century CE they were absorbed into the provinces of Pannonia and Moesia, and the name Singidunum survived as a Roman legionary base.

senones-400.t: Gaulish people of the Adriatic coast of the Marche, credited with the sack of Rome in 390 BCE and destroyed by Rome in 283 BCE.
senones-400.o: The Senones were, according to Polybius and Livy, the last of the Celtic peoples to cross into Italy, around 400 BCE. They settled on the Adriatic coast between the Utente and Esino rivers, land later called the Ager Gallicus, displacing Umbrians and Etruscan settlers.
senones-400.r: They lived in villages and buried their warriors with weapons and imported Etruscan and Greek goods, as at Montefortino and Filottrano. Roman tradition said Senones led by Brennus defeated Rome at the Allia and sacked the city in 390 BCE. They raided central Italy and served as mercenaries, including for Dionysius I.
senones-400.e: The Senones fought alongside the Samnites at Sentinum in 295 BCE. After they defeated a Roman army at Arretium in 284 BCE, Publius Cornelius Dolabella expelled or destroyed them in 283 BCE, and the colony of Sena Gallica (Senigallia) was founded on their land.

smolyani.t: Slavic tribe of the Rhodope Mountains and Mesta valley, known from Byzantine sources until it passed under Bulgarian rule in the 9th century.
smolyani.o: The Smolyani were among the Slavic groups who settled the Balkans in the late 6th and 7th centuries, taking the Rhodopes and the middle Mesta (Nestos) in modern Bulgaria and Greece. They are named among the tribes that besieged Thessalonica in the 670s.
smolyani.r: Known only from brief Byzantine mentions, they were a tribal people under local chiefs, nominally subject to Byzantium, farming and herding in the mountain valleys. The modern town of Smolyan preserves their name.
smolyani.e: In 837 the Smolyani rose against Byzantine rule, and Khan Presian of the First Bulgarian Empire used the revolt to take their lands, which were absorbed into Bulgaria.

siris.t: Short-lived Ionian Greek city on the Gulf of Taranto, proverbial for wealth, destroyed by its Achaean neighbours in the 6th century BCE.
siris.o: Ionian Greeks from Colophon in Asia Minor, fleeing Lydian attacks, founded Siris around 680 BCE near the mouth of the Siris (Sinni) river, apparently taking over an existing native settlement. The poet Archilochus praised its land as fair and lovely.
siris.r: Little is known of its government. Siris was famous for its fertile land and luxury, like its neighbour Sybaris, and became a rival to the Achaean cities of Metapontum, Sybaris and Croton. Some scholars link the hill of Policoro with its main settlement. Herodotus records that Athens later claimed a right to the site.
siris.e: Around 530 BCE an alliance of Metapontum, Sybaris and Croton captured Siris and destroyed it, reportedly killing suppliants at the altar of Athena. In 433 BCE Taras and Thurii founded Heraclea on or near its territory.

septinsular-republic.t: Republic of the Seven Islands under Russian and Ottoman protection, the first self-governing Greek state of modern times.
septinsular-republic.o: In 1798-1799 a joint Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Fyodor Ushakov drove the French from the Ionian Islands. The Treaty of Constantinople in 1800 created the Septinsular Republic of Corfu, Paxos, Lefkada, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Kythira, under Ottoman suzerainty and Russian protection.
septinsular-republic.r: The republic was governed by a senate in Corfu dominated by the island nobility, under a series of constitutions; that of 1803 widened participation. Count Spyridon Theotokis presided over the senate, and the young Ioannis Kapodistrias, later the first governor of Greece, served as secretary of state. Greek became an official language alongside Italian.
septinsular-republic.e: At Tilsit in 1807 Russia ceded the islands to Napoleon, and they returned to French rule as the French Ionian Islands. The republic's experience of self-rule fed the ideas of the Greek national movement.

salassi.t: Alpine people of the Aosta valley who controlled the Great and Little St Bernard passes and their gold, and resisted Rome until 25 BCE.
salassi.o: The Salassi lived in the Aosta valley and around Eporedia (Ivrea), at the foot of the passes over the western Alps. Ancient writers called them Celts, though they probably mixed with earlier Ligurian peoples. They appear in Roman history in the 2nd century BCE.
salassi.r: The Salassi controlled the routes over the Alpine passes, charging tolls on travellers and armies. They worked gold deposits in the Dora Baltea valley by washing, and their disputes with Roman contractors over water rights, recorded by Strabo, led to conflict. They lived in villages and fortified places and had no known central capital.
salassi.e: Appius Claudius Pulcher fought them in 143 BCE, and Rome founded Eporedia in 100 BCE. In 25 BCE Aulus Terentius Varro Murena conquered them for Augustus, selling some 36,000 into slavery, and founded Augusta Praetoria, modern Aosta, on their land.

subalpine-republic.t: A French-controlled republic in Piedmont between Napoleon's victory at Marengo and the region's annexation to France in 1802.
subalpine-republic.o: Napoleon's victory at Marengo in June 1800 restored French control over Piedmont, which had been lost in 1799. The French set up a new government for the former mainland territories of the Kingdom of Sardinia, which became known as the Subalpine Republic.
subalpine-republic.r: The republic was administered by a commission under French supervision, with General Jourdan as administrator general from 1801. It introduced French administrative divisions and laws, abolished remaining feudal rights and prepared Piedmont for annexation. Piedmontese opinion was divided between those favouring France and those hoping for an Italian republic.
subalpine-republic.e: In September 1802 Piedmont was formally annexed to France and divided into French departments. It returned to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1814.

sybaris.t: Achaean Greek city in southern Italy so rich that its name became a byword for luxury, destroyed by its neighbour Croton in 510 BCE.
sybaris.o: Achaean colonists from the northern Peloponnese, led by Is of Helike, founded Sybaris around 720 BCE on the plain between the Crathis and Sybaris rivers, near the Gulf of Taranto. The fertile plain and routes across the Calabrian isthmus to the Tyrrhenian Sea gave it rapid growth.
sybaris.r: Sybaris became one of the largest Greek cities in the West. Strabo says it ruled four native peoples and twenty-five subject towns and could field an enormous army. It founded Poseidonia and other colonies, and its traders worked closely with Miletus and the Etruscans. Later Greek writers delighted in tales of Sybarite excess, which gave English the word 'sybarite'. Around 510 BCE a popular leader, Telys, seized power and expelled the wealthy.
sybaris.e: When Croton sheltered the Sybarite exiles, war followed. In 510 BCE Croton's army, led by the athlete Milo, defeated Sybaris, and the victors are said to have diverted the Crathis over the ruins. Attempts at refoundation led to the Panhellenic colony of Thurii in 444 BCE nearby.

second-hellenic-republic.t: The Greek republic of 1924-1935, born from the Asia Minor disaster and marked by coups, refugee resettlement and the last Venizelos government.
second-hellenic-republic.o: Greece's defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 discredited the monarchy. A military revolution forced Constantine I to abdicate, and in March 1924 the assembly proclaimed a republic, confirmed by a referendum in April. The Kingdom of Greece was thus replaced, with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis as first president.
second-hellenic-republic.r: The republic had to absorb more than a million refugees from Anatolia after the population exchange with Turkey, resettling many in Macedonia. Politics were unstable: General Theodoros Pangalos ruled as dictator in 1925-1926. The Venizelos government of 1928-1932 brought stability, a peace treaty with Turkey and public works, but the Great Depression ended it.
second-hellenic-republic.e: Royalists won the 1933 elections, and a failed Venizelist coup in March 1935 strengthened them. In October 1935 General Georgios Kondylis seized power, and a rigged plebiscite restored the monarchy, bringing back George II.

selgovae.t: People of the Scottish Borders recorded by Ptolemy, whose lands around the Eildon Hills were held by the Roman fort of Trimontium.
selgovae.o: The Selgovae are known from Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography, which places them in southern Scotland, usually located in the upper Tweed valley and the hills of the central Borders. Their name may mean 'the hunters'. They grew from Iron Age communities whose landscape contained many hillforts, including the large enclosure on Eildon Hill North.
selgovae.r: No rulers, coins or written records survive. The heavy Roman military presence around their land, especially the fort of Trimontium at Newstead under the Eildon Hills, has led historians to suggest they were hostile to Rome, in contrast to their neighbours the Votadini. Their society was rural, based on cattle and small farms.
selgovae.e: Roman control of southern Scotland ebbed and flowed between the 80s and the 2nd century, after which the region lay beyond Hadrian's Wall. The Selgovae disappear from the record, their lands later forming part of the British kingdoms of the north.

sordones.t: People of the Roussillon plain beneath the eastern Pyrenees, whose town Ruscino gave the region its name.
sordones.o: Known only from Greek and Roman writers such as Avienus, Pomponius Mela and Pliny, the Sordones held the coastal plain around Ruscino (Château-Roussillon, near Perpignan). Their culture had strong Iberian ties, and their land lay on the coastal route between Iberia and Gaul.
sordones.r: Livy reports that in 218 BCE Gallic chiefs gathered at Ruscino to decide whether to let Hannibal pass on his march to Italy, and he won them over with gifts. Excavations at Ruscino show a hilltop settlement with storage silos and imported Greek and Italian goods.
sordones.e: After 121 BCE the area was absorbed into the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis. Ruscino became a small Roman town with a forum before declining, and its name survives in Roussillon.

second-athenian-league.t: Alliance of Aegean states formed by Athens in 378 BCE to resist Sparta, with promises not to repeat the abuses of the 5th-century empire.
second-athenian-league.o: Spartan high-handedness after the King's Peace of 386 BCE, and a raid on Attica by the Spartan Sphodrias, pushed Athens to found a new alliance in 378-377 BCE. The surviving decree of Aristoteles invites Greeks and barbarians to join 'so that the Spartans may allow the Greeks to be free', listing members such as Chios, Thebes and Byzantium.
second-athenian-league.r: Members kept their autonomy and constitutions, and Athens renounced garrisons, governors, tribute and Athenian settlement on allied land. Allies sat in a council (synedrion) at Athens that voted alongside the Athenian assembly and paid 'contributions' rather than tribute. At its height some seventy states joined. Chabrias' naval victory off Naxos in 376 BCE restored Athenian sea power.
second-athenian-league.e: Athens gradually broke its promises, planting settlers on Samos. In the Social War of 357-355 BCE Chios, Rhodes, Cos and Byzantium, encouraged by Mausolus of Caria, left the league. Reduced to a rump, it ended after Philip II's victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and the creation of the League of Corinth.

second-taifa-of-valencia.t: Valencia's short independence under its qadi after the Almoravid collapse, a prelude to the rise of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King.
second-taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1145 the notables of Valencia expelled the Almoravid governor and recognised their qadi, Marwan ibn Abd al-Aziz, as ruler, part of the wave of urban revolts that ended Almoravid rule in eastern al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-valencia.r: The regime rested on the qadi's prestige and the support of the city's elite, but it lacked troops. Real military power in the east lay with commanders such as Ibn Iyad and, after him, Muhammad ibn Mardanish, who soon pushed the qadi aside.
second-taifa-of-valencia.e: By 1147 Ibn Mardanish had taken control of Valencia and joined it to his realm, the Second Taifa of Murcia, which held out against the Almohads until 1172.

sertorian-state.t: The breakaway Roman regime of Quintus Sertorius, who with Iberian allies held most of Hispania against the Senate for nearly a decade.
sertorian-state.o: Quintus Sertorius, a supporter of Marius, was driven from Hispania by Sulla's forces but returned in 80 BCE at the invitation of the Lusitanians. Combining Roman exiles with Lusitanian and Celtiberian warriors, he defeated Sulla's generals and by 77 BCE controlled much of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.
sertorian-state.r: Sertorius ran a rival Roman state with its own senate of exiles and magistrates, while winning Iberian loyalty through fair treatment and personal charisma, aided by a white fawn said to bring him divine messages. At Osca he founded a school where sons of Iberian nobles learned Latin and Greek, partly as hostages. He allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus and beat Pompey at Lauron in 76 BCE.
sertorian-state.e: Worn down by Metellus Pius and Pompey, his alliance frayed. In 73 or 72 BCE he was murdered at a banquet by his lieutenant Marcus Perperna, whom Pompey soon defeated and executed. Hispania returned to Senate rule.

sabines.t: Italic people of the hills north-east of Rome, central to Roman foundation legends, who were absorbed by Rome in the early 3rd century BCE.
sabines.o: The Sabines lived in the central Apennines and the hill country between the Tiber and the Aniene from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers saw them as the parent stock of several Sabellian peoples, such as the Samnites and Picentes, who were said to have left Sabine land in 'sacred springs' of migration.
sabines.r: Sabine society was rural, made up of villages and small towns such as Cures, Reate, Nursia and Amiternum, with a reputation in Roman eyes for austere virtue. They spoke an Osco-Umbrian language known only from glosses. In Roman legend the abduction of the Sabine women led to joint rule between Romulus and the Sabine king Titus Tatius, and Rome's second king Numa Pompilius came from Cures. The Claudii were said to descend from Attus Clausus, who moved to Rome around 504 BCE.
sabines.e: Manius Curius Dentatus conquered the Sabines in 290 BCE. They received citizenship without the vote, and full citizenship in 268 BCE, an early and complete absorption into the Roman state. Their land was later part of Augustus's Regio IV, and the name survives in the Sabina district north of Rome.
